title: Vanilla pouring custard
summary: A pale, vanilla-scented pouring custard of almond milk and coconut cream, thickened with a whisper of xanthan so it coats a spoon; vegan as written.

ingredients.note: a tiny pinch, for colour only

steps: Warm the almond milk, coconut cream, allulose, salt and turmeric in a saucepan over medium heat, whisking, until steaming and just at a simmer, about 85 °C (185 °F), 4–5 minutes.
Take the pan off the heat. Sprinkle the xanthan gum over the surface a little at a time while blending with a stick blender (or whisking hard), then blend 30 seconds more so no lumps form.
Stir in the vanilla. Rest 2 minutes: it should coat the back of a spoon and hold a clean line when you run a finger through it. If it is thin, blend in another pinch of xanthan.
Serve warm, or press plastic wrap onto the surface and chill; it pours cold too. Keeps 4 days refrigerated; stir before using.
tips: Xanthan thickens without heat or setting, so unlike crème anglaise this cannot curdle or overcook; too much makes it slimy, so add it by the pinch.
For a richer, more set texture, use 0.5 tsp agar instead of the xanthan: boil it with the milks for 2 minutes, chill until set, then blend smooth. It pours cold but thickens again if left still.
It has no egg yolk, so the colour comes from the turmeric and the richness from the coconut cream; it tastes cleaner and lighter than the original.

origin.history: Crème anglaise, 'English cream', is usually said to be named for the English love of pouring custard; milk sauces thickened with egg yolks were made on both sides of the Channel and the sauce was standard in classical French cookery by the 1800s. Egg-free pouring custard has a long history of its own in Britain through Bird's custard powder, created around 1837, reportedly for a wife who could not eat eggs. Today's plant-milk versions thickened with gums or agar extend that idea.
